title: Working with Data: Tables, Graphs, Mean, Median, Mode, Range, Units, and Probability
objectives: You will read data tables and bar and line graphs by checking the title, labels, units, and key.
You will calculate the mean, median, mode, and range of a data set and explain what each measure shows.
You will identify an outlier and choose the measure of center that best describes typical data.
You will calculate rates of change from tables and graphs and convert between common science units.
You will find simple probabilities and use them to predict expected outcomes in science contexts.

slides.title: Working with Data in Science
slides.board:
Today you will:

  • Read tables and graphs: title, labels, units, key
  • Find the mean, median, mode, and range
  • Spot an outlier and pick the best “typical” value
  • Find rates of change and convert units
  • Find probabilities and predict expected outcomes

Plan: Warm-up → 6 big ideas → practice together → your turn → GED-style questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 2 of Science. Last week you learned how scientists design an experiment; this week is about what they do with the numbers that come out of it. Almost every GED Science question shows a table or a graph, and most of the points are lost by misreading the data, not by doing hard math. Today we build a reading routine and a small toolkit: four measures of center and spread, rates, units, and probability.
ask: Where did you last see a graph or a table outside of school, such as a weather app, a food label, or a bill? (expected answer: any example; ask what its title and units were)

slides.title: Warm-Up: Week 1 Review
slides.board:
A student gives tomato plants 0 g, 5 g, or 10 g of fertilizer each week. After 8 weeks she counts the tomatoes on each plant. Each amount is tested on 3 plants.

  1. Name the independent variable and the dependent variable.
  2. Which plants are the control group?
  3. Write a hypothesis for this experiment.
  4. The three 10 g plants grew 14, 17, and 14 tomatoes. Find the mean.
steps: 1. IV: amount of fertilizer (what she changed). DV: number of tomatoes (what she measured).
2. The 0 g plants: they get no fertilizer, so they are the baseline.
3. Example: If tomato plants get more fertilizer, then they will grow more tomatoes, because fertilizer supplies nutrients the plant needs to grow.

notes.say: These four questions review last week: variables, the control group, the hypothesis, and the mean of repeated trials. Give the student about two minutes, then have them tell you each answer before you reveal it. Problem 4 is our bridge into today: the mean is one of the four tools we will use with every data set.
ask: Why does she test each amount on 3 plants instead of 1? (expected answer: repeated trials make the results more reliable; one plant could be unusual)
Name one variable she should keep the same. (expected answer: water, light, soil, pot size, type of tomato plant)
notes.answer: 1. IV: amount of fertilizer; DV: number of tomatoes. 2. The 0 g plants. 3. Any If…, then…, because… statement that predicts how fertilizer affects tomato count. 4. 15 tomatoes.
notes.watch: If the student says the 0 g plants are a “controlled variable,” stop and review: the control group is a group that gets no treatment; controlled variables are conditions kept the same for every group.

slides.title: Big Idea 1: Read Before You Calculate
slides.board:
T-A-U-K before any math:

Title: what is this about?
Axes or column headings: what was measured?
Units: cm, °C, mg/L, beats per minute?
Key: which bar or line is which?

Bar graphLine graph
Compares separate groupsShows change over time
Rainfall in four citiesA plant’s height each week

Steeper line = faster change.

notes.say: Most data mistakes on the GED come from reading, not from arithmetic. So before you calculate anything, read the title, the axes or headings, the units, and the key. Then say in one sentence what the table or graph shows. Bar graphs compare separate categories; line graphs show one thing changing over time, and the steeper the line, the faster the change. The overall direction of a line is called the trend.
ask: Why would a line graph be a poor choice for comparing rainfall in four cities? (expected answer: the cities are separate categories; a line would suggest a change over time that does not exist)
What does a flat part of a line graph mean? (expected answer: no change during that time)
notes.watch: Students often skip the units and the key. Have them point to the heading and the key out loud before they read any value.

slides.title: Worked Example: Read the Table
slides.board:
Stream Depth After a Storm (cm)

Hours after rain02468
Site A4058524744
Site B4045514946

(a) What was the depth at Site B at 4 hours? (b) Which site peaked sooner? (c) When did Site A rise fastest?
steps: T-A-U-K: the table shows stream depth in centimeters at two sites, every 2 hours after a rain. Each row is a site.
(a) Find the Site B row, then the 4-hour column: 51 cm. (58 at 2 hours is Site A, the wrong row.)
(b) Site A’s greatest depth (58 cm) came at 2 hours; Site B’s (51 cm) came at 4 hours. Site A peaked sooner.
(c) Site A changes: +18, −6, −5, −3. The biggest rise is 0 to 2 hours (+18 cm): the steepest part of its line.

notes.say: Watch my routine. First I say what the table is about and what the rows and columns mean. Then, for every value, I put one finger on the row and one on the column. To find when something changed fastest, I subtract neighbors and look for the biggest difference.
ask: What was Site A's depth at 6 hours? (expected answer: 47 cm)
Was there any time when the two sites had the same depth? (expected answer: yes, at 0 hours, both 40 cm)

slides.title: We Do: Describe the Trend
slides.board:
Ice Thickness on a Lake

Week123456
Thickness (cm)2611151718
  1. What is the trend?
  2. Between which two weeks did the ice grow the most?
  3. Bar graph or line graph?
  4. What happens to the growth near the end?
steps: 2. Changes: +4, +5, +4, +2, +1. The most growth was week 2 to week 3 (+5 cm).
3. A line graph: one quantity changing over time.
4. The weekly growth slows down (+2, then +1): the line gets flatter.

notes.say: Let's do this one together. You tell me each change from week to week, and I will write them under the table. Notice that the ice is still getting thicker at the end, but more slowly. 'Increasing' and 'increasing faster' are not the same thing, and the GED likes to test that difference.
ask: What is the change from week 4 to week 5? (expected answer: 17 − 15 = 2 cm)
Is the ice getting thinner at the end? (expected answer: no; it is still getting thicker, just more slowly)
notes.answer: 1. Increasing. 2. Week 2 to week 3 (+5 cm). 3. Line graph. 4. The growth slows down; the line flattens.
notes.watch: Some students answer question 2 with “week 6” because 18 is the greatest value. Ask: “Is the question about the biggest value or the biggest change?”

slides.title: Big Idea 2: Center and Spread
slides.board:
MeasureHow to find itTells you
MeanAdd all values ÷ how manyThe average
MedianPut in order; take the middle (two middles: average them)The middle
ModeValue that appears most oftenMost common
RangeGreatest − leastSpread

notes.say: These four measures answer two different questions. Mean, median, and mode answer 'What is typical?' Range answers 'How spread out are the data?' The step people skip is ordering the data before finding the median. A data set can have one mode, more than one mode, or no mode at all.
ask: Find the median of 7, 3, 9, 1. (expected answer: order 1, 3, 7, 9; (3 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5)
Which measure tells spread instead of center? (expected answer: the range)
notes.watch: Students sometimes report the range as the “typical” value. Keep repeating: range is spread, not center.

slides.title: Worked Example: Resting Heart Rates
slides.board:
A nurse records six adults’ resting heart rates in beats per minute (bpm):

62, 68, 58, 74, 70, 88

Find the mean, median, mode, and range.
steps: Median: order them: 58, 62, 68, 70, 74, 88. Six values, so average the two middle ones: (68 + 70) ÷ 2 = 69 bpm.
Mode: no value appears more than once, so there is no mode.
Check: the mean and median (70 and 69) both fall between 58 and 88.

notes.say: Here is the full toolkit on one data set. Notice that I rewrite the list in order before I look for the median. If I had taken the middle of the unordered list, I would have averaged 58 and 74 and gotten 66, which is wrong. The last step is a reasonableness check: any measure of center must sit between the least and greatest values.
ask: What would the mode be if a seventh person had 70 bpm? (expected answer: 70 bpm)
notes.watch: Watch for students who divide by 5 or 7. Have them count the values out loud before dividing.

  1. Mean water temperature?
  2. Median dissolved oxygen?
  3. Range of dissolved oxygen?

steps: 4. Sort by temperature: 14 (10.2), 16 (9.6), 18 (8.9), 20 (8.1). As temperature increases, dissolved oxygen decreases.

notes.say: This is real field data of the kind the GED loves. Walk me through each one; tell me the step before you tell me the number. For question 4, we have to sort the sites by temperature first, because the table lists them A, B, C, D, not from coldest to warmest. And remember: four sites show a pattern, not proof of cause.
ask: What is the first step for the median? (expected answer: put the oxygen values in order)
Does this table prove warm water causes low oxygen? (expected answer: no; it shows a pattern at four sites, not cause and effect)
notes.answer: 1. 17 °C. 2. 9.25 mg/L. 3. 2.1 mg/L. 4. As water temperature increases, dissolved oxygen decreases.
notes.watch: For question 2, students often average 8.9 and 9.6 straight from the table rows (B and C), which happens to work here. Ask them to order the list anyway, since it will not always work.

slides.title: Big Idea 3: Outliers and the Best “Typical” Value
slides.board:
Outlier: a value far from the rest. It may be a real, unusual result or an error.

An outlier pulls the mean toward it.
The median barely moves.

Data with an outlier → the median usually describes typical data better.

Data with no outlier → the mean is fine.

notes.say: An outlier is one value that sits far away from the others. It might be real, like one unusually large fish, or it might be a mistake, like a contaminated sample. Because the mean adds every value into the sum, one extreme value drags it toward that extreme. The median only cares about position, so it hardly moves. When a GED question asks which value best describes a typical result and you see an outlier, think median.
ask: Five incomes: four are about $40,000 and one is $2 million. Which better describes a typical income, the mean or the median? (expected answer: the median)
notes.watch: Students may think an outlier should always be thrown out. Explain: only remove it if there is a reason, such as an error in the procedure; otherwise report it and use the median.

slides.title: Worked Example: The Uncovered Plate
slides.board:
A student counts bacteria colonies on five plates treated the same way:

41, 44, 39, 42, 104

Plate 5 was left uncovered for an hour. Which value best describes a typical plate?
steps: Median (all five): in order 39, 41, 42, 44, 104. Middle value = 42 colonies.
The mean of 54 is higher than four of the five plates. The median, 42, matches a typical plate. Plate 5 was likely contaminated, which is a good reason to call it an outlier.

notes.say: One plate out of five changed the mean by more than 12 colonies. That is how strongly an outlier pulls the mean. The median stayed at 42, close to every normal plate. Notice that the procedure gave us a reason to suspect plate 5, so we can report the median or the mean without it.
ask: How much did the outlier raise the mean? (expected answer: 54 − 41.5 = 12.5 colonies)

slides.title: Your Turn: Center, Spread, and Outliers
slides.board:
1. Rainfall (mm) on five days: 5, 9, 7, 9, 10. Find the mean, median, mode, and range.
  2. Find the median of 12, 3, 8, 6.
  3. Egg masses (g): 58, 61, 60, 59, 22. The 22 g egg came from a different bird species. Find the mean and median. Which better describes a typical egg?
steps: 1. Mean = 40 ÷ 5 = 8 mm; median (5, 7, 9, 9, 10) = 9 mm; mode = 9 mm; range = 10 − 5 = 5 mm.
3. Mean = 260 ÷ 5 = 52 g; median (22, 58, 59, 60, 61) = 59 g. The median is better: the 22 g outlier pulls the mean below four of the five eggs.

notes.say: Work these alone; you have four minutes. Tell me each answer and how you got it. I will reveal after you commit.
notes.answer: 1. Mean 8 mm, median 9 mm, mode 9 mm, range 5 mm. 2. 7. 3. Mean 52 g, median 59 g; the median is better because the 22 g egg is an outlier.
notes.watch: On problem 2, the unordered middle values are 3 and 8, giving 5.5. If you hear 5.5, ask: “Did you put them in order first?”

slides.title: Big Idea 4: Rates of Change
slides.board:
A rate compares two different units: cm per day, beats per minute. “Per” means divide.

Rate of change = (change in amount) ÷ (change in time)
= (end − start) ÷ (end time − start time)

On a line graph, the steepest section is the fastest change.

notes.say: A rate tells how fast something changes. Say the rate in words first: centimeters per week means centimeters divided by weeks. To find an average rate from a table, subtract the starting amount from the ending amount, subtract the starting time from the ending time, and divide. Always attach the units, because '10.5' alone means nothing.
ask: A puppy weighed 3 kg at week 8 and 7 kg at week 16. What was its average rate of gain? (expected answer: 4 kg ÷ 8 weeks = 0.5 kg per week)
notes.watch: The common error is dividing one reading by the time (for example, 7 ÷ 16) instead of dividing the change. Insist on two subtractions before the division.

slides.title: Worked Example: Sunflower Growth
slides.board:
Week02468
Height (cm)820386280

(a) During which two-week period did the plant grow fastest?
(b) What was the average growth rate from week 2 to week 6?
steps: The largest change, 24 cm, is from week 4 to week 6: the steepest segment of the line.
(b) Change in height: 62 − 20 = 42 cm. Change in time: 6 − 2 = 4 weeks.

notes.say: For part (a), I subtract each pair of neighbors and look for the biggest change. For part (b), I use only the two endpoints the question names. Notice the units on every line. The answer is a rate, centimeters per week, not just a length.
ask: What was the average rate over all 8 weeks? (expected answer: (80 − 8) ÷ 8 = 72 ÷ 8 = 9 cm per week)
notes.watch: Some students divide 62 by 6. Point out that the plant was already 20 cm tall at week 2; only the growth counts.

slides.title: Big Idea 5: Units and Conversions
slides.board:
LengthVolumeMassTime
1 cm = 10 mm
1 m = 100 cm
1 km = 1,000 m		1 L = 1,000 mL1 kg = 1,000 g
1 g = 1,000 mg		1 min = 60 s
1 h = 60 min
1 day = 24 h

Big unit → small unit: multiply.
Small unit → big unit: divide.

notes.say: Science uses the metric system, which is built on tens, hundreds, and thousands. The rule is simple: when you go from a big unit to a small unit, you need more of them, so multiply. When you go from a small unit to a big unit, you need fewer, so divide. Before you finish, ask yourself whether the number should have gotten bigger or smaller.
ask: How many milliliters are in 2.4 liters? (expected answer: 2.4 × 1,000 = 2,400 mL)
How many kilometers is 3,500 meters? (expected answer: 3,500 ÷ 1,000 = 3.5 km)
notes.watch: Watch for multiplying when the units get bigger. Ask: “Should there be more of the new unit, or fewer?”

slides.title: Worked Example: Convert a Rate
slides.board:
(a) The sunflower grew 10.5 cm per week. What is that in millimeters per day?

(b) A patient should drink 1.5 L of water a day. A glass holds 250 mL. How many glasses is that?
steps: (a) Per day: a day is smaller than a week, so divide by 7: 10.5 ÷ 7 = 1.5 cm per day.
Millimeters: a mm is smaller than a cm, so multiply by 10: 1.5 × 10 = 15 mm per day.
(b) Liters to milliliters (big to small, multiply): 1.5 × 1,000 = 1,500 mL.

notes.say: Converting a rate means converting one unit at a time. In part (a), I change weeks to days first, then centimeters to millimeters. In part (b), I must get both amounts into the same unit, milliliters, before I divide. If I had divided 1.5 by 250, I would get a tiny decimal, which makes no sense for glasses of water.
ask: How many glasses would 2 L be? (expected answer: 2,000 ÷ 250 = 8 glasses)

slides.title: We Do: Rates and Units
slides.board:
1. At 6:00 a.m. the air was 52 °F. At 12:00 noon it was 70 °F. What was the average rate of warming?
  2. A sample has a volume of 2.4 L. How many milliliters is that?
  3. A tortoise walks 0.3 km in 2 hours. What is its speed in meters per minute?
steps: 3. 0.3 km × 1,000 = 300 m. 2 h × 60 = 120 min. 300 ÷ 120 = 2.5 m per minute.

notes.say: We will do these together, one unit at a time. For number 3, convert the distance and the time first, then divide. Tell me each conversion and I will write it down. Saying the units out loud keeps us from dividing in the wrong order.
ask: In number 3, what do we divide by what? (expected answer: meters divided by minutes, because the rate is meters per minute)
notes.answer: 1. 3 °F per hour. 2. 2,400 mL. 3. 2.5 m per minute.
notes.watch: On number 3, students may divide 0.3 by 2 and stop (0.15 km per hour). Remind them to read what unit the question asks for.

slides.title: Big Idea 6: Probability and Expected Outcomes
slides.board:
P(event) = favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes
P(not the event) = 1 − P(event)
Expected number = probability × number of tries

Probability is from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).

1/4 = 0.25 = 25%

40% chance of rain → 60% chance of no rain.

notes.say: Probability tells how likely something is, as a fraction, decimal, or percent between 0 and 1. The total always goes on the bottom. The chance something does not happen is 1 minus the chance it does. To predict how many times something will happen, multiply the probability by the number of tries; that gives an expected number, which is an estimate, not a guarantee. Experimental probability comes from data that were collected; theoretical probability comes from equally likely outcomes, like a fair coin.
ask: A forecast gives a 15% chance of frost. What is the chance of no frost? (expected answer: 85%)
What is the probability of rolling a 5 or a 6 on a fair number cube? (expected answer: 2/6 = 1/3)
notes.watch: If a probability comes out greater than 1, the student divided in the wrong order. Have them say “part over total” before dividing.

slides.title: Worked Example: Small-Animal Traps
slides.board:
A biologist sets 50 traps in a meadow. Next morning: 18 hold a mouse, 7 hold a vole, 25 are empty.

(a) P(mouse)? (b) P(any animal)? (c) P(no mouse)? (d) About how many of 200 traps would catch a mouse?
steps: (d) 0.36 × 200 = about 72 traps. This is an expected value, not a guarantee.

notes.say: Every one of these uses the same total: 50 traps. For 'any animal,' I add the mice and voles before I divide. For 'no mouse,' I use the complement, 1 minus the probability of a mouse. And for the prediction, I multiply the probability by the new number of tries.
ask: What is the probability a trap is empty? (expected answer: 25 ÷ 50 = 50%)
notes.watch: For part (c), some students answer 50% (the empty traps). A trap with a vole also has “no mouse,” so P(no mouse) = (7 + 25) ÷ 50 = 64%.

slides.title: Your Turn: Rates and Units
slides.board:
1. A bean plant was 12 cm tall on day 3 and 30 cm tall on day 9. Find its average growth rate.
  2. Convert 750 mL to liters.
  3. Express the rate from problem 1 in millimeters per week.
steps: 3. 3 cm × 10 = 30 mm per day; 30 × 7 = 210 mm per week.

notes.say: Three minutes, on your own. Write the units on every line of work. Tell me your answers and I will reveal them.
notes.answer: 1. 3 cm per day. 2. 0.75 L. 3. 210 mm per week.
notes.watch: On problem 1, listen for 30 ÷ 9 = 3.33. That divides a reading, not the change. On problem 3, check that both conversions went in the multiply direction (cm to mm, day to week).

slides.title: Your Turn: Probability
slides.board:
Volunteers counted 40 birds: 14 sparrows, 10 robins, 16 other birds.

  1. What is the probability that a counted bird was a robin?
  2. What is the probability it was not a robin?
  3. The next survey will count 200 birds. About how many robins are expected?
  4. A forecast gives a 15% chance of frost. What is the chance of no frost?

notes.say: Your turn again; you have three minutes. Give me each answer as a percent. On number 3, tell me why we say 'about.'
notes.watch: On number 1, some students divide 10 by 30 (robins versus all the other birds). The total, 40, goes on the bottom.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: The Best Typical Value
slides.board:
A town measures daily water use (liters) in seven homes: 210, 190, 230, 200, 220, 840, 210. Home 6 has a leaking pipe.

Which value best describes typical daily water use for these homes?

A. The median, 210 L
B. The mean, 300 L
C. The range, 650 L
D. The midpoint of the least and greatest values, 515 L
steps: B is out. The mean (2,100 ÷ 7 = 300 L) is pulled up by the 840 L leak. It is higher than six of the seven homes.
C is out. The range (840 − 190 = 650 L) measures spread, not a typical value.
D is out. (190 + 840) ÷ 2 = 515 L uses only the two extremes, so the outlier pulls it even more than the mean.
A is correct. In order: 190, 200, 210, 210, 220, 230, 840. The middle value, 210 L, sits right among the typical homes.

notes.say: This is the classic outlier question. Before you look at the choices, scan the data for a value that does not fit; here it is the 840 with a leak. Then remember the rule: the outlier drags the mean, the median holds steady. Eliminate the measures of spread and anything built from the extremes.
ask: What would the mean be without home 6? (expected answer: 1,260 ÷ 6 = 210 L)
notes.answer: A. The median, 210 L, is not affected by the leaking home. B is pulled up by the outlier, C measures spread, and D depends only on the extremes.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Compare the Groups
slides.board:
GroupHad symptomsTotal
New allergy treatment30250
Placebo45150

Which statement is supported by the data?

A. Placebo patients were 1.5 times as likely to have symptoms.
B. Placebo patients were 2.5 times as likely to have symptoms.
C. Placebo patients were 18 times as likely to have symptoms.
D. Treatment patients were more likely to have symptoms, since more were tested.
steps: Find each group’s rate using its own total: treatment 30 ÷ 250 = 12%; placebo 45 ÷ 150 = 30%.
A is out. 45 ÷ 30 = 1.5 compares raw counts and ignores that the groups are different sizes.
C is out. 30 − 12 = 18 is a difference in percentage points, not “times as likely.”
D is out. A bigger group does not mean a higher rate; the treatment rate (12%) is lower.

notes.say: When two groups have different sizes, you cannot compare the raw counts. Convert each group to a rate first, dividing by that group's own total. Then 'how many times as likely' means divide one rate by the other, not subtract.
ask: What percent of all 400 patients had symptoms? (expected answer: 75 ÷ 400 = 18.75%)
notes.answer: B. 12% versus 30%, and 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5. A compares raw counts, C subtracts the rates, D ignores the rates entirely.

slides.title: Test Strategy: Estimate Before You Calculate
slides.board:
Before you touch the calculator, take five seconds:

1. T-A-U-K: what are the units?
2. Estimate: a mean or median must sit between the least and greatest values.
3. A probability must be between 0 and 1.
4. After converting, ask: should the number be bigger or smaller?

Then cross out any choice that fails these checks.

notes.say: The GED Science test gives you an on-screen calculator, but the calculator will happily give you a wrong answer if you set it up wrong. Five seconds of estimating protects you. If heart rates are all between 60 and 90, an answer of 420 is the sum and 15 is nonsense. If a probability comes out as 2.5, you divided in the wrong order. Many wrong choices fail one of these checks, so you can often eliminate two choices before you calculate anything.
ask: The data are 14, 17, and 20 grams. Could the mean be 51? (expected answer: no; 51 is the sum. The mean must be between 14 and 20; it is 17)

slides.title: Recap and What Comes Next
slides.board:
1. T-A-U-K first: title, axes, units, key. Bar = compare groups; line = change over time.
  2. Mean = sum ÷ count; median = middle of ordered data; mode = most common; range = greatest − least.
  3. An outlier pulls the mean; the median holds steady.
  4. Rate = change ÷ time. Big unit to small unit: multiply.
  5. P = favorable ÷ total; P(not) = 1 − P; expected = P × tries.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice (Set A) → Exit Check

notes.say: Let's pull it together. Read each takeaway back to me in your own words. Your next step is the Student Lesson, which walks through every idea again with a check on each screen. Then do Practice Set A; if you score under 80 percent, take Set B. Finish with the Exit Check, where you need 6 of 8.
ask: Which measure is best for typical data that has an outlier? (expected answer: the median)
What goes on the bottom of a probability? (expected answer: the total number of outcomes)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
Scientists collect numbers: temperatures, heights, heart rates, counts of animals. On the GED Science test, many questions give you a table or a graph and ask what the data show. You will not need advanced math. You need to read carefully, choose the right calculation, and keep track of units. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • Read a table or graph by checking its title, labels, units, and key.
  • Find the mean, median, mode, and range of a data set.
  • Spot an outlier and choose the best “typical” value.
  • Find a rate of change and convert units.
  • Find a probability and predict an expected number.

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Keep scratch paper and a calculator nearby.

screens.title: Read before you calculate
screens.html:
Most data mistakes come from misreading, not from bad arithmetic. Before you answer anything, check four things. Remember them as T-A-U-K:

  • Title: What is this table or graph about?
  • Axes or column headings: What was measured?
  • Units: centimeters? degrees? milligrams per liter?
  • Key: If there are two bars, lines, or rows, which is which?

Then say in one sentence what the data show. To read one value, put one finger on the row and one on the column, and read where they meet.

check.prompt:
Average Monthly Rainfall (mm)

MonthRivertonDry Gulch
January9214
February8010
March10522
April7018

What was the average rainfall in Dry Gulch in March?
why: 105 mm is Riverton’s March rainfall. You read the wrong column. Find the Dry Gulch heading first, then go down to March.
18 mm is Dry Gulch’s April rainfall. You read the row below March. Keep one finger on the March row.
127 mm is 105 + 22, the two cities added together. The question asks about Dry Gulch only.
check.hint: Find the Dry Gulch column, then the March row. Read where they meet.
check.explain: The table shows average rainfall in millimeters for two cities. The Dry Gulch column and the March row meet at 22 mm. The value 105 mm is in the same row but belongs to Riverton.

screens.title: Bar graphs, line graphs, and trends
screens.html:
Bar graphs compare separate groups, such as the rainfall in four cities or the number of each kind of tree in a forest. The bars can be in any order.

Line graphs show how one quantity changes over time or as another quantity changes, such as a plant’s height each week. The points are connected because each one follows the last.

On a line graph, the trend is the overall direction: increasing, decreasing, or no clear pattern. The steeper the line, the faster the change. A line that is still rising but getting flatter is increasing more slowly.

Recall from Week 1: the independent variable goes on the x-axis, and the dependent variable goes on the y-axis.

check.prompt:
A vet records a puppy’s mass every week for 10 weeks. The masses (kg) are 2.0, 2.6, 3.3, 3.9, 4.4, 4.8, 5.1, 5.3, 5.4, 5.5.

The best way to display these data is a {{0}} graph. The trend is that the puppy’s mass {{1}}, and near the end the line gets {{2}}.

why: A bar graph compares separate groups. These are one puppy’s masses over time, so a line graph shows the change.
A circle graph shows the parts of one whole, such as the percent of people with each blood type. It cannot show a change over time.
Every mass is larger than the one before it, from 2.0 kg to 5.5 kg, so the mass is not decreasing.
The mass changes every week, from 2.0 kg up to 5.5 kg.
The weekly gains shrink at the end (0.2, then 0.1, then 0.1 kg). Smaller changes mean a flatter line, not a steeper one.
A level line would mean the mass stopped changing. The puppy still gains 0.1 kg each week at the end, so the line is still rising, just less steeply.

check.hint: Is this one thing changing over time, or several separate groups? Then look at the size of the weekly changes near the end.
check.explain: The data show one puppy’s mass changing over time, so use a line graph. Every value is larger than the last, so the mass increases. Near the end the weekly gains are only 0.3, 0.2, 0.1, and 0.1 kg, so the line gets flatter: the puppy is still growing, but more slowly.

screens.title: Reading changes in a table
screens.html:
Many questions ask when something changed the most. That is a question about change, not about the biggest value. Subtract each value from the next one, write the changes between the columns, and compare them.

On a line graph, the biggest change is the steepest segment. A decrease is a change too: a drop from 50 to 35 is a change of 15.

example.prompt: A lake’s ice thickness was 2, 6, 11, 15, 17, and 18 cm in weeks 1 through 6. During which week did the ice grow the most?
steps: It happened from week 2 to week 3.
example.answer: From week 2 to week 3 (+5 cm). Week 6 has the greatest thickness, but not the greatest growth.

check.prompt:
Day036912
Seedling height (cm)2.03.56.07.28.0

What was the largest growth between two back-to-back measurements, in centimeters?

mistakes.why: 8.0 cm is the greatest height, not the greatest growth. Subtract each height from the next one and compare the changes.
6 is either the height on day 6 or the total growth from day 0 to day 12 (8.0 − 2.0). The question asks for the largest change between two back-to-back measurements.
1.5 cm is the first change (day 0 to day 3), not the largest. Find all four changes: 1.5, 2.5, 1.2, 0.8.

check.hint: Subtract each height from the next one. Which difference is biggest?
check.explain: Changes: 3.5 − 2.0 = 1.5; 6.0 − 3.5 = 2.5; 7.2 − 6.0 = 1.2; 8.0 − 7.2 = 0.8. The largest is 2.5 cm, from day 3 to day 6. That would be the steepest part of a line graph.

screens.title: The mean
screens.html:
The mean is the average. It is the value each data point would have if the total were shared equally.

Mean = (sum of the values) ÷ (number of values)

Count the values before you divide. A quick check: the mean must be between the least and greatest values. If your answer is bigger than every value, you probably forgot to divide.

example.prompt: A sleep study records how many hours six people slept: 7.5, 6, 8, 5.5, 6, 9. Find the mean.

check.prompt: A student drops a ball four times and measures how high it bounces: 43 cm, 47 cm, 44 cm, and 50 cm. What is the mean bounce height, in centimeters?

mistakes.why: 184 is the sum of the four bounces. Divide the sum by the number of bounces: 184 ÷ 4 = 46.
You divided by 3, but there are four bounces. Divide 184 by 4.
46.5 is halfway between the smallest and largest bounces (43 and 50). The mean uses all four values: 184 ÷ 4 = 46.

check.hint: Add all four heights, then divide by 4.
check.explain: 43 + 47 + 44 + 50 = 184. There are 4 values, so 184 ÷ 4 = 46 cm. Check: 46 is between 43 and 50.

screens.title: The median
screens.html:
The median is the middle value after you put the data in order from least to greatest.

  • Odd number of values: the median is the one in the middle.
  • Even number of values: there are two middle values. The median is their mean (add them and divide by 2).

A good method: write the list in order, then cross off one value from each end until you reach the middle.

example.prompt: Find the median of these sleep times (hours): 7.5, 6, 8, 5.5, 6, 9.
steps: Six values, so the two middle values are 6 and 7.5.

check.prompt: A weather station recorded the hours of sunshine on six days: 7, 9.5, 11, 8, 6.5, 10. What is the median number of hours?

mistakes.why: You may have averaged the two middle values of the unordered list (11 and 8). Put the values in order first: 6.5, 7, 8, 9.5, 10, 11.
8 is only one of the two middle values. With six values, average the two middle ones: (8 + 9.5) ÷ 2 = 8.75.
That is the mean (52 ÷ 6). The median is the middle of the ordered list, not the average of all the values.

check.hint: Put the six values in order. Then average the two in the middle.
check.explain: In order: 6.5, 7, 8, 9.5, 10, 11. There are six values, so the middle two are 8 and 9.5. (8 + 9.5) ÷ 2 = 8.75 hours.

screens.title: Mode and range
screens.html:
The mode is the value that appears most often. A data set can have one mode, more than one mode, or no mode (if no value repeats).

The range is the greatest value minus the least value. It tells how spread out the data are. It is not a “typical” value.

Mean, median, and mode answer “What is typical?” Range answers “How spread out?”

example.prompt: Six people slept 7.5, 6, 8, 5.5, 6, and 9 hours. Find the mode and the range.
steps: Mode: 6 appears twice; every other value appears once. Mode = 6 hours.

check.prompt:
A bird watcher counted the eggs in seven robin nests: 4, 3, 4, 5, 2, 4, 3.

The mode is {{0}} eggs, and the range is {{1}} eggs.

why: 3 appears twice, but 4 appears three times. The mode is the value that appears most often.
5 is the greatest value, and it appears only once. The mode is the most frequent value.
About 3.6 is the mean (25 ÷ 7). The mode is the value that appears most often.
5 is the greatest value. The range is greatest minus least: 5 − 2 = 3.
7 is the number of nests, not the spread of the egg counts.
2 is the least value. Subtract it from the greatest: 5 − 2 = 3.

check.hint: Count how many times each number appears. For the range, subtract the least value from the greatest.
check.explain:
Mode: 4 appears three times (more than any other value), so the mode is 4 eggs.

Range: 5 − 2 = 3 eggs.

screens.title: Outliers
screens.html:
An outlier is a value far away from the rest of the data. It might be a real but unusual result, or it might be an error, such as a misread instrument or a contaminated sample.

An outlier has a big effect on the mean, because it is added into the sum. It has almost no effect on the median, because the median only depends on which value is in the middle.

example.prompt: Five students timed how long a cup of ice took to melt (minutes): 30, 32, 29, 31, 78. One cup was left in the shade by accident.
steps: Mean: 30 + 32 + 29 + 31 + 78 = 200; 200 ÷ 5 = 40 minutes. That is longer than four of the five cups.
Median: in order 29, 30, 31, 32, 78. The middle value is 31 minutes.
The outlier (78) pulled the mean up by about 10 minutes; the median stayed near the typical cups.
example.answer: Mean 40 minutes; median 31 minutes. The median better describes a typical cup.

check.prompt: A data set is 12, 14, 13, 15, and 46. How does the value 46 affect the mean and the median?
options: It raises the mean to 20, but the median stays at 14.
It raises the median to 20, but the mean stays at 14.
It raises both the mean and the median to about 20.
It has no effect on the mean, because one value is too few to matter.
why: This swaps the two measures. The mean is the one that adds in the 46 and jumps to 20; the median is the middle value of the ordered list, 14.
Only the mean jumps. In order (12, 13, 14, 15, 46), the middle value is still 14, so the median barely changes.
The mean adds every value, so one large value matters a lot: (12 + 14 + 13 + 15 + 46) ÷ 5 = 20, compared with 13.5 without the 46.
check.hint: Find the mean and median with the 46 included. Compare them with the other values.
check.explain:
Mean: 12 + 14 + 13 + 15 + 46 = 100; 100 ÷ 5 = 20. Without 46, the mean would be 54 ÷ 4 = 13.5.

Median: in order 12, 13, 14, 15, 46, the middle value is 14. The outlier pulled the mean up, but the median stayed with the typical values.

screens.title: Choosing the best typical value
screens.html:
When a question asks which number best describes a typical value, use this rule:

No outlier: the mean is a good choice.
Outlier present: the median is usually better.

Do not throw out an outlier just because it is inconvenient. Remove it only if there is a reason, such as an error in the procedure. Otherwise, report it and choose the median. Never choose the range for a typical value; it measures spread.

check.prompt: A student measured how far five frogs jumped (cm): 82, 90, 85, 88, and 30. Frog 5 had an injured leg. Which number best describes the typical jump of a healthy frog in this group?
why: The mean (375 ÷ 5 = 75 cm) is pulled down by the injured frog’s 30 cm jump. It is shorter than every healthy frog’s jump.
The range (90 − 30 = 60 cm) tells how spread out the jumps are, not what a typical jump is.
30 cm is the outlier itself, from the injured frog. It is the least typical value in the set.
check.hint: Look for an outlier. Which measure is barely affected by it?
check.explain: The injured frog’s 30 cm jump is an outlier. In order: 30, 82, 85, 88, 90. The median is 85 cm, right among the healthy frogs. The mean, 375 ÷ 5 = 75 cm, is shorter than all four healthy jumps because the outlier pulled it down.

screens.title: Rate of change
screens.html:
A rate compares two quantities with different units, such as centimeters per day or degrees per hour. The word “per” means divide.

Rate of change = (ending amount − starting amount) ÷ (ending time − starting time)

Do two subtractions, then one division. Write the units: the answer is “amount per time.” If the amount went down, say it decreased at that rate.

example.prompt: At 6:00 a.m. the air temperature was 52 °F. At 12:00 noon it was 70 °F. What was the average rate of warming?

check.prompt: During a dry spell, a pond’s water level was 148 cm on day 2 and 124 cm on day 10. What was the average rate at which the water level dropped, in centimeters per day?

mistakes.why: 24 cm is the total drop. Divide it by the number of days that passed: 10 − 2 = 8 days, so 24 ÷ 8 = 3.
You divided by 10, the ending day. The time that passed is 10 − 2 = 8 days.
You divided one reading (124 cm) by the time. Divide the change in level (148 − 124 = 24 cm) by the change in time (8 days).

check.hint: Find the change in level and the change in days. Then divide.
check.explain: Change in level: 148 − 124 = 24 cm. Change in time: 10 − 2 = 8 days. Rate: 24 ÷ 8 = 3 cm per day.

screens.title: Metric unit conversions
screens.html:
Science uses the metric system. These are the conversions you need most:

LengthVolumeMassTime
1 cm = 10 mm
1 m = 100 cm
1 km = 1,000 m		1 L = 1,000 mL1 kg = 1,000 g
1 g = 1,000 mg		1 min = 60 s
1 h = 60 min
1 day = 24 h

Big unit → small unit: multiply (you need more of them).
Small unit → big unit: divide (you need fewer).

example.prompt: A runner drinks 0.75 L of water. How many milliliters is that?
steps: Liters are bigger than milliliters, so multiply.
Check: the number got bigger because milliliters are smaller units.

check.prompt: A rock sample has a mass of 2.4 kg. What is its mass in grams?

mistakes.why: You divided by 1,000. Kilograms are bigger than grams, so there are more grams: multiply, 2.4 × 1,000 = 2,400.
You multiplied by 100. There are 1,000 grams in a kilogram, not 100.

check.hint: 1 kg = 1,000 g. Are you going from a big unit to a small unit?
check.explain: A kilogram is bigger than a gram, so multiply: 2.4 × 1,000 = 2,400 g.

screens.title: Converting a rate
screens.html:
To convert a rate, change one unit at a time. Convert the top unit (the amount), then the bottom unit (the time), or the other way around.

For the time part, think about what happens: in a longer time, more happens, so going from “per minute” to “per hour” means multiply by 60. Going from “per minute” to “per second” means divide by 60.

example.prompt: A sunflower grew 10.5 cm per week. What is that in millimeters per day?
steps: Per day: a day is shorter than a week, so less growth happens. 10.5 ÷ 7 = 1.5 cm per day.
Millimeters: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 1.5 × 10 = 15 mm per day.

check.prompt: A garden snail crawls at about 6 cm per minute. What is that speed in meters per hour?
why: 360 is the number of centimeters per hour (6 × 60). You still need to change centimeters to meters: 360 ÷ 100 = 3.6.
0.06 m is how far the snail goes in one minute. You converted centimeters to meters but did not change minutes to hours (multiply by 60).
You divided 360 by 10 instead of 100. There are 100 centimeters in a meter.
check.hint: First find centimeters per hour (an hour has 60 minutes). Then change centimeters to meters (100 cm = 1 m).
check.explain: Per hour: 6 cm × 60 = 360 cm per hour. To meters: 360 ÷ 100 = 3.6 meters per hour.

screens.title: Probability
screens.html:
Probability tells how likely an event is. It is a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), written as a fraction, decimal, or percent: 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%.

P(event) = (number of favorable outcomes) ÷ (total number of outcomes)

Theoretical probability comes from equally likely outcomes, such as a fair coin or number cube. Experimental probability comes from data that were collected, such as a survey or a set of trials. The total always goes on the bottom.

example.prompt: In a bird survey, volunteers counted 40 birds: 14 sparrows, 10 robins, and 16 other birds. What is the probability that a counted bird was a robin?

check.prompt: A bird feeder camera recorded 50 visits: 18 by chickadees, 22 by finches, and 10 by cardinals. What is the probability that a randomly chosen visit was by a finch? Enter the answer as a percent.

mistakes.why: 22 is the number of finch visits, not the probability. Divide by the total: 22 ÷ 50 = 0.44 = 44%.
0.44 is the correct probability written as a decimal. The question asks for a percent: 0.44 × 100 = 44%.
56% is the probability the visit was not by a finch (28 ÷ 50). The question asks for finches.
You divided 22 by 28, the visits by the other birds. The total, 50, goes on the bottom.

check.hint: Divide the finch visits by the total visits, then change the decimal to a percent.

screens.title: “Not” and expected numbers
screens.html:
Two more tools:

P(event does not happen) = 1 − P(event)
Expected number = probability × number of tries

A forecast of a 40% chance of rain means a 60% chance of no rain. If 25% of birds in a survey are robins, then in a new survey of 200 birds you would expect about 0.25 × 200 = 50 robins. An expected number is a prediction, not a guarantee; real counts vary a little.

example.prompt: A seed company’s tests show that 85% of its seeds sprout. A gardener plants 60 seeds. About how many will not sprout?

check.prompt: In a lab population of fruit flies, 4% have white eyes. A student examines a sample of 650 flies. About how many flies in the sample are expected to have white eyes?

mistakes.why: 624 is the number expected not to have white eyes (96% of 650). The question asks about white eyes: 0.04 × 650 = 26.
You multiplied by 4 instead of 4%. Write 4% as a decimal, 0.04, before multiplying.
You divided 650 by 4. Finding 4% means multiplying by 0.04, not dividing by 4 (that would be 25%).

check.hint: Change 4% to a decimal. Then multiply by the number of flies.
check.explain: 4% = 0.04. Expected number = 0.04 × 650 = 26 flies. Check: 1% of 650 is 6.5, and 4 × 6.5 = 26.

screens.title: Comparing groups of different sizes
screens.html:
Studies often compare two groups that are not the same size. You cannot compare the raw counts. Instead, find the rate (probability) within each group, dividing by that group’s own total.

To say how many times as likely, divide one rate by the other. Subtracting the rates tells you the difference in percentage points, which is a different thing.

example.prompt: Of 400 vaccinated adults, 12 got the flu. Of 300 unvaccinated adults, 45 got the flu. How many times as likely was an unvaccinated adult to get the flu?

check.prompt:
GroupSeeds plantedSeeds that sprouted
Fertilizer X5040
Fertilizer Y7554

Which group had the higher sprouting rate?
options: Fertilizer X, because 80% of its seeds sprouted, compared with 72%
Fertilizer Y, because 54 of its seeds sprouted, compared with only 40
Fertilizer Y, because 54 ÷ 40 shows its rate was 1.35 times as high
Neither one, because groups of different sizes cannot be compared
why: 54 is a bigger count, but Y also planted more seeds. Compare rates: 54 ÷ 75 = 72%, which is lower than X’s 40 ÷ 50 = 80%.
54 ÷ 40 compares raw counts from groups of different sizes. Divide each count by its own group’s total first.
Groups of different sizes can be compared by converting each to a rate (a percent).
check.hint: Divide each group’s sprouted seeds by that group’s seeds planted.
check.explain: X: 40 ÷ 50 = 0.80 = 80%. Y: 54 ÷ 75 = 0.72 = 72%. Fertilizer X had the higher sprouting rate, even though Y had more seeds sprout in total.

screens.title: Stay inside the data
screens.html:
A conclusion must be supported by the data shown. Watch for three traps:

  • Going past the data. Predicting far beyond the range that was measured is a guess, not a supported conclusion.
  • Claims about things not measured. If the table shows chirps per minute, it says nothing about why crickets chirp.
  • Cause from a pattern. Two things changing together does not prove one causes the other, unless an experiment changed only that one variable.

Words like always, only, and proves are warning signs.

check.prompt:
A student counted how many times a cricket chirped per minute at different temperatures.

Temperature (°C)15202530
Chirps per minute6295128160

Which statements are supported by the data? Select two answers.
options: As the temperature increased, the chirp rate increased.
At 25 °C, the cricket chirped about twice as often as at 15 °C.
At 40 °C, the cricket will chirp about 225 times per minute.
Temperature is the only factor that controls how often crickets chirp.
Crickets chirp more in warm weather to attract mates.
why: No data were collected above 30 °C. This prediction goes far past the measured range.
Only temperature was tested. The data cannot show that nothing else matters, and “only” is a warning sign.
The table shows chirp rates, not the reason crickets chirp. Mating was never measured.
check.hint: Check each statement against the numbers. Was it actually measured?
check.explain:
Every time the temperature went up, the chirp rate went up (62, 95, 128, 160), so the statement that the chirp rate increased is supported. At 25 °C the rate was 128, and 128 ÷ 62 ≈ 2.1, so “about twice” is supported.

The 40 °C prediction goes beyond the data, “only factor” was never tested, and the reason for chirping was never measured.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• T-A-U-K first: title, axes or headings, units, key. Bar graphs compare groups; line graphs show change over time; steeper means faster.
  • Mean = sum ÷ count. Median = middle of the ordered data (two middles: average them). Mode = most frequent. Range = greatest − least (spread, not center).
  • Outlier: pulls the mean; the median barely moves. With an outlier, the median is usually the better typical value.
  • Rate = change in amount ÷ change in time. Big unit to small unit: multiply. Convert one unit at a time.
  • Probability = favorable ÷ total, from 0 to 1. P(not) = 1 − P. Expected number = P × tries. Compare groups of different sizes by their rates.
  • Conclusions stay inside the data.

Routine for every data question: read T-A-U-K, estimate, calculate, then check the answer against the data and its units.

items.prompt: What was the range of the daily high temperatures for the week?
why: 74 °F is only the least value (Friday). The range is greatest minus least: 87 − 74 = 13.
81 °F is the mean, which measures the center, not the spread. Range = greatest − least.
87 °F is only the greatest value (Sunday). Subtract the least value from it: 87 − 74 = 13.
items.hint: Range = greatest value minus least value.
items.explain:
The greatest high temperature was 87 °F (Sunday). The least was 74 °F (Friday).

Range = 87 − 74 = 13 °F.

87 °F is only the greatest value, and 74 °F is only the least. 81 °F is the mean, which measures center, not spread. The range always uses both extremes.

items.prompt: What was the mean daily high temperature for the week? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 567 is the sum of the seven temperatures. Divide by the number of days: 567 ÷ 7 = 81.
You divided by 6, but there are seven days. Divide 567 by 7.
82 °F is the median (and the mode), not the mean. The mean adds all seven values and divides by 7.

items.hint: Add all seven high temperatures, then divide by 7.

78 + 82 + 85 + 79 + 74 + 82 + 87 = 567

Check: 81 is between the least (74) and greatest (87) values, so it is reasonable. Forgetting to divide (567) or dividing by 6 (94.5) gives a value outside that range.

items.prompt: Between which two back-to-back minutes did the volunteer’s heart rate drop the most?
why: The drop from minute 2 to minute 3 is 118 − 106 = 12 bpm. The drop from minute 0 to minute 1 is larger, 18 bpm.
From minute 3 to minute 4 the heart rate fell 106 − 98 = 8 bpm, one of the smaller drops. Subtract each pair and compare.
Minute 5 to minute 6 has the smallest drop (92 − 88 = 4 bpm), where the line is flattest. You may have looked for the lowest heart rate instead of the biggest change.
items.hint: Subtract each heart rate from the one before it, or look for the steepest part of the line.
items.explain:
Find the drop for each minute:

  • 0 to 1: 150 − 132 = 18 bpm
  • 1 to 2: 132 − 118 = 14 bpm
  • 2 to 3: 118 − 106 = 12 bpm
  • 3 to 4: 106 − 98 = 8 bpm
  • 4 to 5: 98 − 92 = 6 bpm
  • 5 to 6: 92 − 88 = 4 bpm

The largest drop, 18 bpm, was between minute 0 and minute 1, the steepest part of the line. Minute 5 to minute 6 had the smallest drop; the line is flattening out there even though the heart rate is lowest.

items.prompt: According to the graph, which flower color received the most visits from butterflies?
why: Purple has the tallest bee bar (34 visits). Use the key: butterflies made only 6 visits to purple flowers.
White has the fewest butterfly visits (2), not the most.
Yellow has the most visits when bees and butterflies are added together (42). The question asks about butterflies only, and butterflies made 12 visits to yellow.
items.hint: Use the key to find the butterfly bars. Then find the tallest one.
items.explain:
T-A-U-K: the graph shows the number of visits to four flower colors, and the key separates bees from butterflies. The butterfly bars are 12 (yellow), 6 (purple), 2 (white), and 20 (red). Red has the most butterfly visits.

The most tempting wrong answer is purple, which has the tallest bar on the whole graph. That bar belongs to the bees.

items.prompt: Which statements are supported by the data? Select two answers.
options: The median high temperature is equal to the mode of the high temperatures.
The warmest day of the week was also the rainiest day.
The total rainfall for the week was 1.80 inches.
It rained on more than half of the days.
The mean high temperature was greater than the median high temperature.
The high temperature rose every day of the week.
why: The warmest day was Sunday (87 °F), which had no rain. Thursday (1.20 inches) was the rainiest day.
It rained on only 3 of the 7 days (Tuesday, Thursday, Friday). That is less than half.
The mean is 81 °F and the median is 82 °F, so the mean is less than the median.
The high fell on Thursday (85 to 79) and Friday (79 to 74), so it did not rise every day.
items.hint: Order the temperatures to find the median and mode. Add the rainfall column.
items.explain:
Median and mode: In order, the highs are 74, 78, 79, 82, 82, 85, 87. The middle (4th) value is 82, so the median is 82 °F. The value 82 appears twice, so the mode is 82 °F. They are equal: supported.

Total rainfall: 0.00 + 0.20 + 0.00 + 1.20 + 0.40 + 0.00 + 0.00 = 1.80 inches: supported.

The others are not supported. The warmest day (Sunday) had no rain. It rained on 3 of 7 days. The mean (81 °F) is less than the median (82 °F). The temperature fell on Thursday and Friday.

items.prompt: What was the average rate at which the volunteer’s heart rate decreased during the first 4 minutes after stopping?
why: 24.5 is 98 ÷ 4. You divided the heart rate at minute 4 by the time instead of dividing the change in heart rate.
37.5 is 150 ÷ 4. You divided the starting heart rate by the time instead of dividing the change, 150 − 98 = 52.
52 bpm is the total drop over the 4 minutes (150 − 98). Divide it by the 4 minutes to get the rate.
items.hint: Rate of change = change in heart rate ÷ change in time. Use minute 0 and minute 4.
items.explain:
Heart rate at minute 0: 150 bpm. Heart rate at minute 4: 98 bpm.

Change in heart rate: 150 − 98 = 52 bpm. Change in time: 4 − 0 = 4 minutes.

Rate: 52 ÷ 4 = 13 bpm per minute (the heart rate fell by 13 beats per minute, each minute).

52 is the total drop, not the rate. 37.5 (150 ÷ 4) and 24.5 (98 ÷ 4) each divide a single reading by the time instead of dividing the change.

items.prompt:
A ruby-throated hummingbird’s heart can beat about 1,200 times per minute while it is flying.

At that rate, its heart beats {{0}} times per second, and {{1}} times in one hour of flying.

why: You multiplied by 60. A second is shorter than a minute, so fewer beats happen in it: divide, 1,200 ÷ 60 = 20.
You subtracted 60. Converting minutes to seconds means dividing by 60, not subtracting it.
You divided 60 by 1,200, which is upside down. Divide the beats by the seconds: 1,200 ÷ 60 = 20.
You added 60. An hour has 60 minutes, so multiply: 1,200 × 60 = 72,000.
20 is the number of beats per second. An hour is longer than a minute, so multiply by 60.
You multiplied by 3,600, the number of seconds in an hour. The rate is per minute, so multiply by the 60 minutes in an hour.

items.hint: 1 minute = 60 seconds and 1 hour = 60 minutes. A shorter time means fewer beats; a longer time means more.
items.explain:
Per second: A second is shorter than a minute, so there are fewer beats in it. 1,200 ÷ 60 = 20 beats per second.

Per hour: An hour is 60 minutes, so multiply: 1,200 × 60 = 72,000 beats.

Choosing 72,000 for the first blank multiplies when you should divide.

items.prompt: A scientist wants to display each data set below. Drag each data set into the type of graph that would display it best.

items.why: The most common mistake is putting the rainfall in four cities on a line graph because rainfall is a weather measurement. The four cities are separate categories with no order in time, so a bar graph compares them.
items.hint: Does the data set show one thing changing over time, or does it compare separate categories?
items.explain:
Line graphs show how one quantity changes over time: body temperature each hour, sunflower height each week, and carbon dioxide level each year.

Bar graphs compare separate categories: kinds of trees, different cities, and blood types. Connecting these categories with a line would suggest a trend that does not exist.

items.prompt: In a lesson on natural selection, a class models a beetle population with 20 beads in a bag: 6 brown, 9 green, and 5 yellow. A student draws one bead without looking. What is the probability that the bead is not green?
why: 45% (9 ÷ 20) is the probability of drawing green, the opposite of what was asked. Use 1 − 0.45, or count the 11 beads that are not green.
30% (6 ÷ 20) is the probability of brown only. Not green includes brown and yellow beads.
25% (5 ÷ 20) is the probability of yellow only. Not green includes brown and yellow beads.
items.hint: Count the beads that are not green, then divide by the total number of beads.
items.explain:
Beads that are not green: 6 brown + 5 yellow = 11. Total beads: 6 + 9 + 5 = 20.

P(not green) = 11 ÷ 20 = 0.55 = 55%.

You can also use the complement: P(green) = 9 ÷ 20 = 45%, so P(not green) = 100% − 45% = 55%. Choosing 45% answers the opposite question.

items.prompt: A seed company’s tests show that 85% of its tomato seeds sprout. A community garden plants 240 of these seeds. About how many seeds are expected to sprout? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 36 is the number expected not to sprout (15% of 240). The question asks how many will sprout: 240 − 36 = 204.
You multiplied by 85 instead of 85%. Write 85% as the decimal 0.85 first: 0.85 × 240 = 204.

items.hint: Expected number = probability × number of tries. Write 85% as a decimal first.
items.explain:
Write the percent as a decimal: 85% = 0.85.

Expected number = 0.85 × 240 = 204 seeds.

Check: 10% of 240 is 24, so 15% is 36, and 240 − 36 = 204. A common error is finding the 36 seeds that do not sprout and stopping there.

items.prompt: The biologist wants one number that best describes the typical length of all six fish she caught. Which choice is best?
options: The median, 15.5 cm, because it is not pulled upward by the 45 cm fish
The mean, about 20.3 cm, because it is the only measure that uses every value
The range, 31 cm, because it includes both the shortest and the longest fish
The mean of the shortest and longest fish, 29.5 cm, because it balances the extremes
why: The mean does use every value, but that is the problem here: the 45 cm outlier pulls it up to about 20.3 cm, longer than five of the six fish.
The range measures how spread out the lengths are, not what a typical fish is like.
(14 + 45) ÷ 2 = 29.5 cm uses only the two extremes, so the outlier pulls it even more than it pulls the mean.
items.hint: Look for an outlier. Which measure of center is affected least by one extreme value?
items.explain:
Fish 6 (45 cm) is an outlier: it is about three times as long as the others.

Median: In order: 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 45. The two middle values are 15 and 16, so the median is (15 + 16) ÷ 2 = 15.5 cm, close to five of the six fish.

Mean: 14 + 16 + 15 + 17 + 15 + 45 = 122; 122 ÷ 6 ≈ 20.3 cm. That is longer than five of the six fish; the outlier pulled it upward.

The range (45 − 14 = 31 cm) measures spread, not a typical value.

items.prompt: Next summer the student plans to record 200 butterfly visits in the same garden bed. If butterflies choose flower colors in the same proportions as in the graph, about how many of those 200 visits are expected to be to yellow flowers? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 30% is the probability that a butterfly visit was to yellow (12 ÷ 40). You still need to multiply by the 200 visits: 0.30 × 200 = 60.
You multiplied the 12 yellow visits by 200. First find the probability, 12 ÷ 40 = 0.3, then multiply by 200.
You divided 12 by 128, all bee and butterfly visits. The question is about butterfly visits only, so the total is 12 + 6 + 2 + 20 = 40.

items.hint: First find the probability that a butterfly visit was to yellow, using only the butterfly bars. Then multiply by 200.
items.explain:
Butterfly visits: 12 (yellow) + 6 (purple) + 2 (white) + 20 (red) = 40.

P(yellow) = 12 ÷ 40 = 0.3.

Expected yellow visits = 0.3 × 200 = 60 visits.

The most common error is dividing by all 128 visits, which mixes in the bees.

items.prompt: Based on the table, a randomly chosen person who was not vaccinated was about how many times as likely to be diagnosed with the flu as a randomly chosen person who was vaccinated?
why: 3.75 is 45 ÷ 12, which compares raw counts and ignores that the groups have different sizes (300 and 400).
12 comes from subtracting the percents (15 − 3). That is a difference in percentage points, not “how many times.”
1.3 is 400 ÷ 300, which compares the group sizes and says nothing about the flu.
items.hint: Find the probability of flu within each group by dividing by that group’s total, not by 700. Then compare the two probabilities.
items.explain:
Find the probability of flu within each group:

  • Vaccinated: 12 ÷ 400 = 0.03 = 3%
  • Not vaccinated: 45 ÷ 300 = 0.15 = 15%

Compare: 15% ÷ 3% = 5 times as likely.

3.75 (45 ÷ 12) compares raw counts from groups of different sizes, and 12 is a difference, not a ratio.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: As water temperature increases from 0 °C to 30 °C, the amount of dissolved oxygen the water can hold decreases.
For every 10 °C increase in temperature, the dissolved oxygen the water can hold decreases by the same amount.
Water at 40 °C would hold no dissolved oxygen at all, because the line is falling toward zero.
Fish grow faster in warm water than in cold water, because warm water helps their bodies work faster.
why: The drops are not equal: 3.3, then 2.2, then 1.5 mg/L. The decrease gets smaller as the water warms.
No data were collected at 40 °C, and the shrinking drops suggest the value would not reach zero. This goes beyond the data.
The table shows dissolved oxygen, not fish growth. Fish growth was never measured, so the data cannot support this.
items.hint: Check each statement against the numbers. For the statement about equal decreases, calculate each 10-degree change.
items.explain:
Every time the temperature goes up, dissolved oxygen goes down: 14.6 → 11.3 → 9.1 → 7.6 mg/L. So dissolved oxygen decreases as temperature increases over the range tested.

The decreases are not equal: 14.6 − 11.3 = 3.3; 11.3 − 9.1 = 2.2; 9.1 − 7.6 = 1.5 mg/L. The line curves rather than falling by the same amount.

No data were collected at 40 °C, and fish growth was never measured.

items.prompt: A leaking faucet in a school lab drips about 15 mL of water per minute. At this rate, how many liters of water leak in one full day (24 hours)? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 21,600 is the number of milliliters. The question asks for liters: 21,600 ÷ 1,000 = 21.6.
0.9 L is the amount that leaks in one hour (15 × 60 = 900 mL). Multiply by 24 hours for a full day.
You multiplied 15 by 24 hours, but the rate is per minute. First multiply by 60 to get mL per hour.

items.hint: Find mL per hour (60 minutes), then mL per day (24 hours), then change mL to L.
items.explain:
Per hour: 15 mL × 60 = 900 mL.

Per day: 900 mL × 24 = 21,600 mL.

To liters (small unit to big unit, divide): 21,600 ÷ 1,000 = 21.6 L.

Leaving the answer as 21,600 forgets that the question asks for liters.

items.prompt: What was the range of the daily low temperatures for the week?
why: 22 °F is only the least value (Thursday). The range is greatest minus least: 36 − 22 = 14.
28 °F is the mean, which measures the center, not the spread.
36 °F is only the greatest value (Saturday). Subtract the least value: 36 − 22 = 14.
items.hint: Find the greatest and least low temperatures. Subtract.
items.explain:
The greatest low temperature was 36 °F (Saturday). The least was 22 °F (Thursday).

Range = 36 − 22 = 14 °F.

The range measures spread, so it needs both extremes. 28 °F is the mean, a measure of center.

items.prompt: What was the mean daily low temperature for the week? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 196 is the sum of the seven low temperatures. Divide by the number of days: 196 ÷ 7 = 28.
You divided by 6, but there are seven days. Divide 196 by 7.
27 °F is the median (the middle value in order), not the mean. Add all seven values and divide by 7.

items.hint: Add all seven low temperatures, then divide by 7.
items.explain:
25 + 31 + 24 + 22 + 31 + 36 + 27 = 196

196 ÷ 7 = 28 °F.

Check: 28 is between 22 and 36.

items.prompt: Between which two back-to-back readings did the volunteer’s blood glucose level change the most?
why: From 30 to 60 minutes the level fell 145 − 125 = 20 mg/dL. You may have picked it because 145 is the peak, but the rise just before it was bigger.
From 60 to 90 minutes the level fell 22 mg/dL, the largest drop. A change can be a rise or a fall, and the rise from 0 to 30 minutes (60 mg/dL) is larger.
From 90 to 120 minutes the level fell only 103 − 91 = 12 mg/dL, the smallest change. The line is flattening out there.
items.hint: Find each change (rise or fall). Which is biggest? On the graph, look for the steepest segment.
items.explain:
Changes between readings:

  • 0 to 30: 145 − 85 = +60 mg/dL
  • 30 to 60: 125 − 145 = −20 mg/dL
  • 60 to 90: 103 − 125 = −22 mg/dL
  • 90 to 120: 91 − 103 = −12 mg/dL

The biggest change is the rise of 60 mg/dL between 0 and 30 minutes, the steepest part of the line. The 22 mg/dL drop from 60 to 90 minutes is the biggest decrease, but it is smaller than the rise.

items.prompt: According to the graph, which seed type was chosen most often by sparrows?
why: Thistle has the tallest finch bar (26 visits). Use the key: sparrows visited thistle only 9 times.
Peanut has the fewest sparrow visits (3), not the most.
Sunflower has the most visits when finches and sparrows are added together (40). The question asks about sparrows only, and sparrows chose sunflower 16 times.
items.hint: Use the key to find the sparrow bars. Then find the tallest one.
items.explain:
The sparrow bars are 16 (sunflower), 22 (millet), 9 (thistle), and 3 (peanut). Sparrows chose millet most often.

The most tempting wrong answer is thistle, which has the tallest bar on the graph, but that bar belongs to the finches.

items.prompt: Which statements are supported by the data? Select two answers.
options: The mode of the low temperatures is greater than the median low temperature.
The coldest day of the week was also the snowiest day.
The total snowfall for the week was 8.0 inches.
It snowed on more than half of the days.
The mean low temperature was less than the median low temperature.
The low temperature fell every day from Monday to Thursday.
why: The coldest day was Thursday (22 °F) with 2.5 inches of snow. The snowiest day was Wednesday (4.0 inches).
It snowed on only 3 of the 7 days (Wednesday, Thursday, Sunday). That is less than half.
The mean is 28 °F and the median is 27 °F, so the mean is greater than the median.
The low rose from 25 °F on Monday to 31 °F on Tuesday, so it did not fall every day.
items.hint: Order the temperatures to find the median and mode. Add the snowfall column.
items.explain:
Median and mode: In order: 22, 24, 25, 27, 31, 31, 36. The median (4th value) is 27 °F. The mode is 31 °F (it appears twice). 31 > 27, so the statement that the mode is greater than the median is supported.

Total snowfall: 0.0 + 0.0 + 4.0 + 2.5 + 0.0 + 0.0 + 1.5 = 8.0 inches: supported.

The coldest day (Thursday) was not the snowiest (Wednesday). It snowed on 3 of 7 days. The mean (196 ÷ 7 = 28 °F) is greater than the median. The low rose on Tuesday.

items.prompt: What was the average rate at which the volunteer’s blood glucose level decreased from 30 minutes to 90 minutes?
why: 42 mg/dL is the total drop (145 − 103). Divide it by the 60 minutes that passed.
About 2.4 is 145 ÷ 60. You divided the reading at 30 minutes by the time instead of dividing the change in glucose.
About 1.7 is 103 ÷ 60. You divided the reading at 90 minutes by the time instead of dividing the change, 145 − 103 = 42.
items.hint: Rate = change in glucose ÷ change in time. Use the readings at 30 and 90 minutes.
items.explain:
At 30 minutes: 145 mg/dL. At 90 minutes: 103 mg/dL.

Change in glucose: 145 − 103 = 42 mg/dL. Change in time: 90 − 30 = 60 minutes.

Rate: 42 ÷ 60 = 0.7 mg/dL per minute.

42 is the total drop, not the rate. Dividing a single reading by 60 (2.4 or 1.7) skips the subtraction.

items.prompt:
An adult at rest breathes in about 6 liters of air per minute.

At that rate, the person breathes in about {{0}} milliliters of air per second, and {{1}} liters of air in one hour.

why: 0.1 is the number of liters per second (6 ÷ 60). The blank asks for milliliters: 0.1 L × 1,000 = 100 mL.
6,000 mL is the amount in one minute. Divide by 60 to get the amount per second.
You multiplied 6,000 mL by 60. A second is shorter than a minute, so divide by 60.
You divided by 60. An hour is longer than a minute, so more air is breathed in: multiply, 6 × 60 = 360.
You added 60. An hour has 60 minutes, so multiply: 6 × 60 = 360.
You multiplied by 3,600, the number of seconds in an hour. The rate is per minute, so multiply by 60.

items.hint: Change liters to milliliters (1 L = 1,000 mL) and minutes to seconds or hours (60 in each step).
items.explain:
Per second: 6 L = 6,000 mL per minute. A second is shorter than a minute, so divide: 6,000 ÷ 60 = 100 mL per second.

Per hour: An hour is 60 minutes, so multiply: 6 × 60 = 360 L.

items.prompt: A pond survey net caught 40 animals: 14 tadpoles, 16 water beetles, and 10 snails. One of these animals is chosen at random. What is the probability that it is not a water beetle?
why: 40% (16 ÷ 40) is the probability that it is a water beetle, the opposite of what was asked.
35% (14 ÷ 40) is the probability of a tadpole only. Not a water beetle includes tadpoles and snails.
25% (10 ÷ 40) is the probability of a snail only. Not a water beetle includes snails and tadpoles.
items.hint: Add the animals that are not water beetles, then divide by the total.
items.explain:
Animals that are not water beetles: 14 + 10 = 24. Total: 40.

P(not a water beetle) = 24 ÷ 40 = 0.6 = 60%.

Or use the complement: P(beetle) = 16 ÷ 40 = 40%, so P(not beetle) = 100% − 40% = 60%.

items.prompt: A fish hatchery finds that 92% of its trout eggs hatch. The hatchery places 350 eggs in a tank. About how many eggs are expected to hatch? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 28 is the number expected not to hatch (8% of 350). The question asks how many will hatch: 350 − 28 = 322.
You multiplied by 92 instead of 92%. Write 92% as the decimal 0.92: 0.92 × 350 = 322.

items.hint: Change 92% to a decimal. Multiply by the number of eggs.
items.explain:
92% = 0.92. Expected number = 0.92 × 350 = 322 eggs.

Check: 8% of 350 is 28, and 350 − 28 = 322.

items.prompt: The student wants one number that best describes how many days a typical seed in this group took to sprout. Which choice is best?
options: The median, 6 days, because it is not pulled upward by the seed that took 21 days
The mean, about 8.3 days, because it is the only measure that uses every value
The range, 16 days, because it includes both the fastest and the slowest seed
The mean of the fastest and slowest seeds, 13 days, because it balances the extremes
why: The mean uses every value, so the 21-day outlier pulls it up to about 8.3 days, longer than five of the six seeds took.
The range measures how spread out the times are, not a typical time.
(5 + 21) ÷ 2 = 13 days uses only the two extremes, so the outlier pulls it even more than it pulls the mean.
items.hint: Is there an outlier? Which measure of center does it affect least?
items.explain:
Seed 6 (21 days) is an outlier, and the notes give a reason: it was planted far too deep.

Median: In order: 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 21. The two middle values are 6 and 6, so the median is 6 days, right among the typical seeds.

Mean: 6 + 5 + 7 + 6 + 5 + 21 = 50; 50 ÷ 6 ≈ 8.3 days, longer than five of the six seeds took.

The range (21 − 5 = 16 days) measures spread, not a typical value.

items.prompt: Next month the student expects to record 150 sparrow visits at the same feeder. If sparrows choose seed types in the same proportions as in the graph, about how many of those 150 visits are expected to be to sunflower seed? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 32% is the probability that a sparrow visit was to sunflower (16 ÷ 50). Multiply it by the 150 visits: 0.32 × 150 = 48.
You multiplied the 16 sunflower visits by 150. First find the probability, 16 ÷ 50 = 0.32, then multiply.
You divided 16 by 106, all finch and sparrow visits. The question is about sparrows only, so the total is 16 + 22 + 9 + 3 = 50.

items.hint: Use only the sparrow bars to find the probability of sunflower. Then multiply by 150.
items.explain:
Sparrow visits: 16 (sunflower) + 22 (millet) + 9 (thistle) + 3 (peanut) = 50.

P(sunflower) = 16 ÷ 50 = 0.32.

Expected sunflower visits = 0.32 × 150 = 48 visits.

Dividing by all 106 visits mixes in the finches, which the question does not ask about.

items.prompt: Based on the table, a randomly chosen camper who did not use sunscreen was about how many times as likely to get a sunburn as a randomly chosen camper who used sunscreen daily?
why: 4 is 36 ÷ 9, which compares raw counts and ignores that the groups have different sizes (200 and 300).
15 comes from subtracting the percents (18 − 3). That is a difference in percentage points, not “how many times.”
1.5 is 300 ÷ 200, which compares the group sizes and says nothing about sunburn.
items.hint: Find the sunburn rate within each group by dividing by that group’s total. Then divide one rate by the other.
items.explain:
Sunburn rate in each group:

  • Used sunscreen: 9 ÷ 300 = 0.03 = 3%
  • No sunscreen: 36 ÷ 200 = 0.18 = 18%

Compare: 18% ÷ 3% = 6 times as likely.

Comparing raw counts (36 ÷ 9 = 4) ignores that the no-sunscreen group was smaller.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: As altitude increases from 0 m to 6,000 m, the air pressure decreases.
For every 2,000 m increase in altitude, the air pressure decreases by the same amount.
At an altitude of 8,000 m there would be no air pressure at all, because the line is falling.
People breathe faster at high altitudes than at sea level, because the air pressure is lower there.
why: The drops are not equal: 21.8, then 17.9, then 14.4 kPa. The decrease gets smaller as altitude increases.
No data were collected at 8,000 m, and the shrinking drops suggest the pressure would not reach zero. This goes beyond the data.
The table shows air pressure, not breathing rate. Breathing was never measured, so the data cannot support this.
items.hint: Check each statement against the numbers. For the statement about equal decreases, calculate each 2,000 m change.
items.explain:
Each time the altitude goes up, the air pressure goes down: 101.3 → 79.5 → 61.6 → 47.2 kPa. So air pressure decreases as altitude increases over the range shown.

The decreases are not equal: 101.3 − 79.5 = 21.8; 79.5 − 61.6 = 17.9; 61.6 − 47.2 = 14.4 kPa.

No data were given for 8,000 m, and breathing rate was never measured.

items.prompt: A hospital IV pump delivers fluid to a patient at 2 mL per minute. How many liters of fluid does the pump deliver in 12 hours? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 1,440 is the number of milliliters. The question asks for liters: 1,440 ÷ 1,000 = 1.44.
0.12 L is the amount in one hour (2 × 60 = 120 mL). Multiply by 12 hours.
You multiplied 2 by 12 hours, but the rate is per minute. First multiply by 60 to get mL per hour.

items.hint: Find mL per hour, then mL in 12 hours, then change mL to L.
items.explain:
Per hour: 2 mL × 60 = 120 mL.

In 12 hours: 120 mL × 12 = 1,440 mL.

To liters: 1,440 ÷ 1,000 = 1.44 L.

vocab.def: Facts or measurements collected during an experiment or study.
vocab.example: The daily high temperatures recorded at a weather station.

vocab.def: An organized display of data in rows and columns with headings and units.
vocab.example: A table listing each day and that day's rainfall in inches.

vocab.def: A graph that uses bars to compare amounts in separate categories.
vocab.example: Bars showing the number of each tree species in a forest plot.

vocab.def: A graph that uses connected points to show how a quantity changes over time or with another quantity.
vocab.example: A line showing a patient's temperature every hour.

vocab.def: The part of a graph that shows which bar, line, or color stands for which data set.
vocab.example: A key showing dark bars for bees and light bars for butterflies.

vocab.def: The overall direction of data: increasing, decreasing, or staying about the same.
vocab.example: Heart rate decreases steadily after exercise stops.

vocab.def: The average: the sum of the values divided by the number of values.
The middle value when the data are put in order. For an even number of values, the mean of the two middle values.
The value that appears most often in a data set.
The difference between the greatest and least values; a measure of spread.
vocab.example: For 58 to 88 bpm, the range is 30 bpm.

vocab.def: A value that is much higher or lower than the rest of the data.
vocab.example: Colony counts of 41, 44, 39, 42, and 104; 104 is an outlier.

vocab.def: A comparison of two quantities with different units, such as distance per time.
vocab.example: A sunflower growing 1.5 cm per day.

vocab.def: Changing a measurement from one unit to another without changing its size.
A number from 0 to 1 that tells how likely an event is: favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
vocab.example: The probability of rolling a 6 on a fair number cube is 1/6.

vocab.def: The number of times an outcome is predicted to happen: probability times the number of tries.
vocab.example: With a 0.36 chance per trap, about 0.36 × 200 = 72 of 200 traps catch a mouse.

notes:
Study Notes: Working with Data

Read First: T-A-U-K

Title • Axes / headings • Units • Key

Bar graph = compare categories. Line graph = change over time. Steeper line = faster change. IV on x-axis, DV on y-axis.

Center and Spread

  • Mean = sum ÷ number of values
  • Median = middle of ordered data (even count: average the two middle values)
  • Mode = most frequent (can be none or more than one)
  • Range = greatest − least (spread, not center)

Outlier: pulls the mean; median barely moves. With an outlier, the median is usually the better "typical" value.

Rates

Rate = change in amount ÷ change in time
"per" means divide. Keep units: cm/day, bpm, mg/L.

Probability

P = favorable ÷ total (0 to 1)
P(not) = 1 − P
Expected = P × number of tries
1/4 = 0.25 = 25%

Two groups of different sizes: find each group’s rate (divide by its own total), then divide the rates for “how many times as likely.”

Temperature

°F = (°C × 9/5) + 32

LengthVolumeMassTime
1 cm = 10 mm; 1 m = 100 cm; 1 km = 1,000 m1 L = 1,000 mL1 kg = 1,000 g; 1 g = 1,000 mg1 min = 60 s; 1 h = 60 min; 1 day = 24 h

Big unit to small unit: multiply. Small unit to big unit: divide. Convert a rate one unit at a time (10.5 cm/week ÷ 7 = 1.5 cm/day = 15 mm/day).

Example data: 58, 62, 68, 70, 74, 88 (bpm). Mean = 420 ÷ 6 = 70. Median = (68 + 70) ÷ 2 = 69. Mode = none. Range = 88 − 58 = 30.

Watch out: order data before finding the median • read the right row and units • total goes on the bottom of a probability • expected values are estimates • do not extend a trend far past the data.
